title: The GLP-1 budget equation
summary: An employer can negotiate a lower price and still spend more overall. The budget depends on how many members receive treatment and how many paid treatment months accumulate. This analysis separates market observations, clinical evidence and a reproducible model of pharmacy spending.

blocks.text: 2. Three quantities drive the pharmacy bill
Annual pharmacy cost = treated members × paid months per treated member × net plan cost per paid month

Treated members means unique members with paid treatment during the budget year. Paid months captures exposure within that year, including start timing and interruptions. It is not a clinical adherence measure.

blocks.text: This model fixes enrollment, drug mix and benefit design. Program fees, medical offsets and productivity effects belong in separate components of a full budget.
3. One price cut, three budget outcomes
Every input below is an assumption, not an observed employer result or a price quote. Enrollment is fixed at 10,000 covered members for 12 months.
Illustrative model
How a 25% price cut becomes a 25% spending increase

blocks.alt: How a 25% price cut becomes a 25% spending increase
blocks.caption: Sequential attribution: change price, then treated-member count, then months. The allocation depends on this order; the total does not. Original chart: YNK Tech; generated from the cited data.

blocks.text: At unchanged use, the price cut lowers annual pharmacy spending from $1.08 million to $810,000. Increasing treated-member count by 50% brings spending to $1.215 million, or 12.5% above baseline. Increasing average paid months from nine to ten raises spending to $1.35 million, or 25% above baseline.

blocks.text: Longer treatment may support health benefits. Its budget effect should be assessed alongside clinical outcomes. These sensitivity cases do not predict how use responds to a lower price.
4. The limit of price negotiation
A 25% price reduction allows 33.3% more paid treatment months at unchanged pharmacy spending: 1 ÷ 0.75 − 1. The expansion scenario increases those months from 1,800 to 3,000, or 66.7%.

blocks.text: 5. Clinical benefit and financial break-even are different outcomes

SELECT found cardiovascular events in 6.5% versus 8.0% over a mean 39.8 months. Participants had established cardiovascular disease, overweight or obesity, and no diabetes. Novo Nordisk funded the randomized trial. [5]

blocks.text: CVS reports lower medical spending but higher total costs in matched Aetna comparisons. Its roughly $350 monthly break-even is model-specific. Separate follow-up samples and residual confounding limit interpretation. This is an industry white paper. [3]

blocks.text: These studies use different populations and methods. They cannot supply one universal medical-offset assumption. Clinical effectiveness also does not, by itself, establish cost effectiveness or employer savings.

The expansion scenario adds $270,000 in pharmacy spending, or $2.25 PMPM. Holding other costs fixed, an equal additional medical saving would be required to keep total plan costs unchanged relative to baseline. This is a break-even requirement, not an estimated saving.

6. Test the mechanism with actual claims

rows: Prior 12-month baseline; enrollment, indications, drug mix and rebate accruals
Establish a consistent starting point; 30 days is a proposed setup window
Net cost per standardized paid month; unique users; paid months per user; pharmacy PMPM
Separate price, participation and duration; compare actuals with approved budget assumptions
Estimated and received rebates; reversals; program fees; benefit changes
Reconcile cash timing and cost attribution; explain remaining variance
Risk-adjusted medical spending and clinical outcomes against a matched comparator
Assess emerging offsets; follow-up duration alone cannot establish causality

blocks.text: Normalize 28- and 30-day supplies consistently. Remove reversals and overlapping paid days; respect enrollment windows. Stratify indications and products. Count rebates once. Paid days do not prove consumption. This monitoring schedule is a proposed design, not a forecast.

The diagnostic finding: lower unit prices improve affordability, while total pharmacy spending depends on treatment volume. Employer evaluation needs separate views of price, paid treatment months, total cost and clinical outcomes.
Methods and limits

Diagnostic synthesis with a deterministic one-year sensitivity model. No scenario probabilities are assigned. No client or patient-level data were used. Enrollment stays at 10,000 for 12 months. Excluded costs are not assumed to be zero in reality. Survey estimates, observational associations, trial findings and modeled thresholds remain distinct. Sources and access limitations are recorded in the accompanying package.
